text: Ford introduces the Model T. Simple, tough and cheap, it put America on wheels; more than 15 million were built by 1927.
Japan opens the Tokaido Shinkansen between Tokyo and Osaka, the world's first high-speed 'bullet train' line, days before the Tokyo Olympics.
In London, John Logie Baird transmits the first television picture of a recognizable human face: office boy William Taynton.
The first successful V-2 rocket launch, at Peenemunde, Germany, climbs about 50 miles high. Its designers later built America's moon rockets.
The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite. Ham radio operators around the world tuned in to its beeps.
The World Series is broadcast on radio for the first time; Grantland Rice covers the games for Pittsburgh's KDKA.
The Reno Gang robs an Ohio & Mississippi Railroad train near Seymour, Indiana: the first robbery of a moving train in the United States.
Soviet probe Luna 3 photographs the far side of the Moon, the first look at the half never seen from Earth.
The Washington, the first double-decker steamboat, arrives at New Orleans: the pattern for the Mississippi riverboats that followed.
On the same dry, windy night the Great Chicago Fire starts and the Peshtigo Fire in Wisconsin kills more than 1,200, the deadliest wildfire in U.S. history.
Joshua Stoddard of Worcester, Massachusetts, patents the steam calliope, soon the loud voice of riverboats and circus parades.
President Wilson presses a telegraph key in Washington, setting off the blast that breaches the Gamboa dike and floods the Panama Canal's Culebra Cut.
Apollo 7 launches: the first crewed Apollo flight, and the first live TV broadcast from an American spacecraft.
Columbus's expedition makes landfall in the Bahamas after more than two months at sea.
The Continental Congress votes to fit out two armed vessels: the birth of what became the U.S. Navy.
Capt. Chuck Yeager flies the Bell X-1 'Glamorous Glennis' faster than the speed of sound over the Mojave Desert.
The airship Graf Zeppelin lands at Lakehurst, New Jersey, completing the first transatlantic flight by an aircraft carrying paying passengers.
The Nickel Plate Road (the New York, Chicago and St. Louis Railroad) runs its first trains over its whole 513-mile line from Buffalo to Chicago.
The Radio Corporation of America (RCA) is founded, keeping American radio patents in American hands after World War I.
Texas Instruments and Regency announce the TR-1, the first commercial transistor radio. Price: $49.95.
George Pullman dies in Chicago. His sleeping cars set the standard for overnight rail travel.
Gen. Douglas MacArthur wades ashore on Leyte, keeping his promise to return to the Philippines.
Nelson's fleet defeats the French and Spanish at Trafalgar; Nelson is killed aboard HMS Victory.
Andre-Jacques Garnerin makes the first parachute jump from a balloon, about 3,200 feet above Paris.
Apple introduces the iPod: '1,000 songs in your pocket.'
The first transcontinental telegraph line is completed. The Pony Express shuts down two days later.
Off Samar, the escort carriers and destroyers of 'Taffy 3' turn back a far larger Japanese fleet in the Battle of Leyte Gulf.
The Erie Canal opens, linking the Great Lakes to the Hudson River and New York City.
New York City's first subway line opens, run by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company (IRT).
Ironworkers set the final section of the Gateway Arch in place, completing St. Louis's 630-foot arch.
The first message crosses ARPANET, the internet's forerunner, from UCLA to Stanford. 'LOGIN' crashed after 'LO'.
Orson Welles's 'War of the Worlds' on CBS radio convinces some listeners that Martians have landed in New Jersey.
A German U-boat sinks the destroyer USS Reuben James off Iceland: the first U.S. Navy warship lost in WWII, five weeks before Pearl Harbor.
At 7:35 a.m., Army Signal Service observers across the country take the first synchronized weather readings and telegraph them to Washington: the start of the National Weather Service.
KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcasts the Harding-Cox presidential election returns, the night the pioneering station counts as its beginning.
Howard Hughes flies his giant wooden H-4 Hercules, the 'Spruce Goose', for about a mile at 70 feet over the water at Long Beach, California. It never flew again.
The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 2 with the dog Laika aboard, the first animal to orbit the Earth.
On election night the UNIVAC I computer, working from a small sample of the vote, predicts an Eisenhower landslide. CBS doubted it and aired a closer call. UNIVAC was right.
George Selden is granted U.S. patent 549,160 for a gasoline automobile, 16 years after he filed. Henry Ford beat the patent in court in 1911.
Edwin Armstrong presents his first paper on FM radio, a way to cut static with frequency modulation, to the Institute of Radio Engineers in New York.
At 9:22 a.m. Donald Smith drives the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Craigellachie, British Columbia.
Operation Torch: American and British forces land in French Morocco and Algeria, opening the U.S. fight against Germany and Italy.
The Great Lakes Storm of 1913, the 'White Hurricane', reaches its peak. In four days it destroyed 19 ships and killed more than 250 people.
The ore carrier Edmund Fitzgerald sinks in a storm on Lake Superior, about 17 miles from Whitefish Bay. All 29 men aboard are lost.
U.S. Route 66 is established, running from Chicago through St. Louis and on to the California coast.
The Armistice Day Blizzard strikes the Midwest after a mild morning. It kills 154 people, many of them duck hunters caught along the Mississippi River.
Space Shuttle Columbia launches on STS-2: the first time a crewed, reusable spacecraft returns to orbit.
The Holland Tunnel opens under the Hudson River between Jersey City and Manhattan: the world's first mechanically ventilated tunnel.
A Japanese submarine torpedoes the cruiser USS Juneau off Guadalcanal. Among the 687 men lost are the five Sullivan brothers of Waterloo, Iowa.
Eugene Ely flies a Curtiss biplane off a platform on the cruiser USS Birmingham: the first airplane takeoff from a ship.
Apollo 12 is struck by lightning twice in its first minute of flight. 'Try SCE to AUX' brings the data back, and the crew lands on the Moon five days later.
Edward Calahan unveils the first stock ticker in New York City, a telegraph printer that sends share prices over the wires.
Intel advertises the 4004 in Electronic News: 'a new era of integrated electronics'. It is the first microprocessor sold for general use.
John Ambrose Fleming applies for a U.S. patent on his 'oscillation valve', the two-electrode vacuum tube that became a foundation of radio.
The Suez Canal opens, joining the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. It cuts about 5,500 miles off the voyage between London and the Arabian Sea.
At noon, North American railroads switch to standard time zones, replacing some 50 separate railroad times.
Ford announces the end of the Edsel. Only 118,287 were built.
Microsoft releases Windows 1.0, a graphical environment that runs on top of MS-DOS.
Over Paris, Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes make the first untethered human flight: 25 minutes and about 5 miles in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon.
Pan American's flying boat China Clipper takes off from Alameda, California, for Manila with the first transpacific airmail.
After 76 hours of fighting, U.S. Marines declare Betio island in Tarawa Atoll secure. The 2nd Marine Division took more than 3,000 casualties.
Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, receives his patent for barbed wire, the cheap fencing that changed ranching on the open range.
The U.S. Navy commissions USS Enterprise, the world's first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.
J.B. Sutherland of Detroit is granted a U.S. patent for an 'Improved Refrigerator-Car', an early step toward shipping fresh food by rail.
New York's Pennsylvania Station opens in full, bringing Pennsylvania Railroad trains into Manhattan through tunnels under the Hudson River.
Frank Duryea wins the Chicago Times-Herald race, the first known automobile race in the U.S.: 54 miles through snow at an average of 5 miles per hour.
Hams span the Atlantic: Fred Schnell (1MO) and John Reinartz in Connecticut make the first two-way amateur contact with Leon Deloy (8AB) in France, on 110 meters.
Richard Byrd and three crewmen fly over the South Pole in the Ford Trimotor 'Floyd Bennett', an 18-hour, 41-minute round trip.
Atari releases Pong, the coin-operated table-tennis game that became the first commercially successful video game.
Samuel Clemens, later Mark Twain, is born in Florida, Missouri. He grew up in Hannibal and worked as a Mississippi riverboat pilot.
Britain's Flying Scotsman becomes the first steam locomotive officially recorded at 100 miles per hour.
The Louisiana Purchase Exposition, the St. Louis World's Fair, closes in Forest Park after seven months and more than 19 million visitors.
Under the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, Enrico Fermi's team starts Chicago Pile-1: the first human-made self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.
Engineer Neil Papworth sends the first text message, from a computer to a Vodafone phone in Britain. It reads 'Merry Christmas'.
The National Grange of the Order of Patrons of Husbandry is founded: the oldest national farm organization in the United States.
The brigantine Dei Gratia finds the Mary Celeste adrift and deserted between the Azores and Portugal. No one from her crew was ever found.
Flight 19, five Navy Avenger torpedo bombers from Fort Lauderdale, vanishes on a training flight. All 14 airmen are lost, and 13 more in a search plane.
The French cargo ship Mont-Blanc collides with the Imo in Halifax harbour and explodes, killing at least 1,782 people: the largest human-made explosion up to that time.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor. All eight U.S. battleships present are damaged, four are sunk, and 2,403 Americans are killed.
Apollo 17 lifts off at 12:33 a.m. Eastern, the only night launch of a Saturn V and the last crewed flight to the Moon.
Eli Whitney is born in Westborough, Massachusetts. His cotton gin of 1793 reshaped the farm economy of the South.
Samuel Langley's Aerodrome collapses on launch and falls into the Potomac River for the second time. Nine days later the Wright brothers fly.
In San Francisco, Douglas Engelbart's 90-minute demonstration shows the computer mouse, windows, hypertext and video conferencing: 'the Mother of All Demos'.
Japanese bombers sink HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Repulse off Malaya, the first capital ships sunk solely by air power while steaming at sea.
Apollo 17's lunar module lands in the Taurus-Littrow valley: the most recent time people have set foot on the Moon.
On Signal Hill in Newfoundland, with an antenna held up by a kite, Marconi reports hearing the Morse letter S sent from Cornwall, about 2,200 miles away.
Francis Drake leaves Plymouth with five ships. He returned in September 1580, having sailed around the world.
Mariner 2 passes about 21,600 miles from Venus: the first spacecraft to successfully encounter another planet.
Gemini 6A, flown by Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford, closes to within one foot of Gemini 7: the first crewed rendezvous in space.
At 2:15 a.m. the first of the great New Madrid earthquakes strikes the Mississippi valley. The shaking was felt as far away as Canada, and the river briefly ran backward.
Germany launches its Ardennes offensive, the Battle of the Bulge: the largest and bloodiest single battle fought by the United States in World War II.
Near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright flies 120 feet in 12 seconds. Wilbur's fourth flight of the day covers 852 feet in 59 seconds.
The Douglas DST, prototype of the DC-3 airliner, makes its first flight, 32 years to the day after the Wright brothers.
Gaston de Chasseloup-Laubat sets the first recognized automobile land speed record at Acheres, France: 39.2 miles per hour in a Jeantaud electric car.
SCORE, the world's first purpose-built communications satellite, is launched. It relayed a recorded greeting from President Eisenhower from orbit.
The BBC Empire Service, today's World Service, begins shortwave broadcasts from Daventry, England.
France hands New Orleans to the United States under the Louisiana Purchase. St. Louis held its own transfer ceremony, Three Flags Day, in March 1804.
Apollo 8 launches with Borman, Lovell and Anders: the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth's gravity and reach the Moon.
At Bastogne, Brig. Gen. Anthony McAuliffe answers a German demand to surrender with one word: 'NUTS!'
At Bell Labs, Walter Brattain demonstrates a working point-contact transistor to colleagues and managers: often given as the birth date of the transistor.
By his own account, Reginald Fessenden broadcasts music and a Bible reading from Brant Rock, Massachusetts, to ships at sea. Historians still argue whether it happened.
In orbit around the Moon, the Apollo 8 crew reads from Genesis on live television and photographs Earthrise.
The locomotive Best Friend of Charleston makes its inaugural run in South Carolina. Its railroad ran the first scheduled steam passenger trains in the United States.
A surprise blizzard finishes burying New York City: 26.4 inches of snow in Central Park, and 77 deaths across the Northeast.
HMS Beagle sails from Plymouth under Robert FitzRoy with the naturalist Charles Darwin aboard. The voyage lasted nearly five years.
Scotland's Tay Rail Bridge collapses in a gale as a passenger train crosses it. Everyone aboard is killed; 59 deaths were confirmed.
Thomas Edison is granted U.S. patent 465,971 for signaling without wires between elevated plates on masts: an early wireless telegraph.
The U.S. signs the Gadsden Purchase, paying Mexico $10 million for land in today's southern Arizona and New Mexico, wanted for a southern railroad to the Pacific.
The ironclad USS Monitor sinks in a storm off Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, while under tow. Sixteen of her crew are lost.
The Homestead Act takes effect, offering settlers 160 acres of public land if they live on it and farm it. Daniel Freeman is credited with the first claim.
Flag day on the ARPANET: TCP/IP replaces the older Network Control Protocol as the network's standard.
President Nixon signs the Emergency Highway Energy Conservation Act, setting a national speed limit of 55 miles per hour.
Apple Computer, Inc. is incorporated, nine months after Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne started the company as a partnership.
NASA's rover Spirit lands in Gusev crater on Mars. Planned to last 90 Martian days, it kept working for more than six years.
Ford announces the Five-Dollar Day: five dollars for an eight-hour shift, in place of just over two dollars for nine hours.
George Washington Carver dies at Tuskegee, Alabama. Born in Diamond, Missouri, he taught Southern farmers crop rotation and promoted peanuts and sweet potatoes in place of cotton.
At the Speedwell Iron Works in New Jersey, Alfred Vail and Samuel Morse send a telegraph message through two miles of wire: 'A patient waiter is no loser.'
The last spike of the Great Northern Railway is driven at Scenic, Washington. The line reached the Pacific without federal land grants.
Commercial telephone service opens between New York and London, carried across the Atlantic by radio. AT&T president Walter Gifford makes the first call.
Ground is broken at the foot of K Street in Sacramento for the Central Pacific Railroad, the western half of the first transcontinental railroad.
Herman Hollerith is granted U.S. patent 395,782 for tabulating punched cards by machine. His machines counted the 1890 census; his company later became part of IBM.
At Macworld, Steve Jobs introduces the iPhone: a widescreen iPod, a mobile phone and an internet device in one. It went on sale that June at $499.
London's Metropolitan Railway opens: the world's first underground passenger railway. Steam locomotives pull gas-lit wooden carriages, and 38,000 people ride on the first day.
Project Diana: Army Signal Corps engineers in New Jersey bounce a radio signal off the Moon and hear the echo about 2.5 seconds later.
Meeting in St. Louis, a state convention votes 60 to 4 to abolish slavery in Missouri, eleven months before the 13th Amendment was ratified.
Amelia Earhart leaves Honolulu in her Lockheed Vega bound for Oakland, California: the first solo flight from Hawaii to the mainland.
The Schoolhouse Blizzard strikes the Great Plains after a mild morning, catching children in one-room schools. An estimated 235 people died.
Lee de Forest broadcasts Enrico Caruso from New York's Metropolitan Opera. Little of the singing came through, but it is regarded as the birth of public radio broadcasting.
The Casablanca Conference opens in Morocco. Roosevelt reached it in a Boeing 314 flying boat, the first aircraft to carry a sitting U.S. president.
The Pennsylvania Railroad's Federal, its brakes cut off, runs through the end of the track at Washington Union Station. GG1 No. 4876 drops through the floor. No one is killed.
Soyuz 4 and Soyuz 5 make the first docking of two crewed spacecraft. Two cosmonauts spacewalk from one ship to the other.
At 11 a.m. the submarine USS Nautilus leaves her pier at Groton, Connecticut, and signals: 'Underway on nuclear power.'
Eugene Ely lands a Curtiss pusher on a wooden platform on the cruiser USS Pennsylvania: the first airplane landing on a ship. Ropes weighted with sandbags stop him.
Apple announces the Lisa, the first mass-market computer worked through a graphical interface and a mouse. Price: $9,995.
Harry Truman's inauguration is the first to be televised. About 10 million people watch.
The first production DeLorean is announced at the factory in Dunmurry, Northern Ireland: unpainted stainless-steel body, gull-wing doors. About 9,000 were built.
At Spearfish, South Dakota, a chinook wind lifts the temperature from -4 F to 45 F in two minutes, still a world record. Later that morning it fell 58 degrees in 27 minutes.
Apple's '1984' commercial, directed by Ridley Scott, airs during Super Bowl XVIII to announce the Macintosh.
After a collision off Nantucket, wireless operator Jack Binns of the liner Republic sends the distress call CQD. About 1,500 people are saved: the first major sea rescue made possible by radio.
Jacques Piccard and Navy Lt. Don Walsh ride the bathyscaphe Trieste to the floor of the Challenger Deep, nearly seven miles down. The descent takes almost five hours.
Apple introduces the Macintosh: 128K of memory, a 9-inch screen and a mouse. Price: $2,495.
Alexander Graham Bell in New York calls Thomas Watson in San Francisco to open transcontinental telephone service.
McDonnell Aircraft of St. Louis flies its XFD-1 Phantom for the first time, with only one of its two engines fitted. It became the first pure jet to land on a U.S. aircraft carrier.
The Great Blizzard of 1978 crosses the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes with gusts to 111 mph. The barometer at Mount Clemens, Michigan, falls to 28.23 inches.
Fire sweeps the Apollo 1 cabin during a launch rehearsal at Cape Kennedy, killing astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee.
The first revenue train runs the full length of the Panama Railroad, about 48 miles from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Space Shuttle Challenger breaks apart 73 seconds after liftoff on a freezing Florida morning. All seven crew members are lost.
Karl Benz applies for German patent 37435 on his three-wheeled Motorwagen with a one-cylinder gasoline engine.
U.S. Army Rangers, Alamo Scouts and Filipino guerrillas raid the Cabanatuan prison camp, 30 miles behind Japanese lines, and bring out more than 500 prisoners.
At 10:48 p.m. Eastern, Explorer 1 lifts off from Cape Canaveral: the first U.S. satellite. Its Geiger counter led to the discovery of the Van Allen radiation belt.
A blizzard that began the evening before leaves 13.9 inches of snow at St. Louis and more than 20 nearby, with five hours of thundersnow at Lambert Field.
Old rivals the Pennsylvania Railroad and the New York Central merge as Penn Central. It filed for bankruptcy in June 1970, the largest U.S. corporate failure up to that time.
Space Shuttle Columbia breaks apart over Texas and Louisiana during re-entry, its left wing damaged by foam at launch. All seven astronauts are lost.
Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, holds its first formal Groundhog Day. Studies since put the groundhog's forecasts at 35 to 41 percent correct.
Grand Central Terminal opens in New York City, built by and named for the New York Central Railroad.
A U-boat torpedoes the troopship Dorchester off Newfoundland. Four Army chaplains give their life jackets to others and go down with the ship; 674 men die.
Charles Lindbergh is born in Detroit. In 1927, backed by St. Louis businessmen, he flew the Spirit of St. Louis alone from New York to Paris in just over 33 hours.
The BBC broadcasts the Greenwich Time Signal for the first time: six short pips counting up to the hour. They have gone out daily ever since.
Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments files for a patent on 'Miniaturized electronic circuits': the integrated circuit. It earned him a Nobel Prize in 2000.
On the Moon with Apollo 14, Alan Shepard hits two golf balls with a six-iron head fixed to a sampling tool. The second, he says, went 'miles and miles and miles.'
John Deere is born in Rutland, Vermont. A blacksmith, he made his first polished steel plow at Grand Detour, Illinois, to cut the sticky prairie soil that clogged iron plows.
Bruce McCandless leaves Space Shuttle Challenger with a jet backpack and no safety line, flying about 320 feet from the ship: the first untethered spacewalk.
The Nasdaq opens as the world's first electronic stock market: no trading floor, just price quotes on computer screens.
President Grant signs the resolution creating a national weather service, placed in the Army Signal Service's Division of Telegrams and Reports for the Benefit of Commerce.
RCA Victor presents Glenn Miller with the first gold record, for 1,200,000 copies of 'Chattanooga Choo Choo.'
In Philadelphia, IBM's Deep Blue wins a game against world chess champion Garry Kasparov, a first for a computer under tournament conditions. Kasparov won the match 4-2.
Thomas Edison is born in Milan, Ohio. He learned telegraphy as a boy selling papers on the trains out of Port Huron, and worked nights as a railroad telegrapher.
Six cars from four nations leave Times Square in the New York to Paris Race. The American Thomas Flyer, driven by George Schuster, reached Paris on July 30 and won.
Warsaw, Missouri, records 40 degrees below zero, still the coldest temperature measured in the state. Warsaw also holds Missouri's record high: 118 F in 1954.
Lawyers for Alexander Graham Bell and Elisha Gray both file telephone papers at the U.S. Patent Office on the same day. Bell got the patent, No. 174,465, three weeks later.
ENIAC is announced to the public: 18,000 vacuum tubes, more than 30 tons. In a demonstration it works out a missile's trajectory in 15 seconds. The press calls it a 'Giant Brain.'
Auguste Chouteau and 30 men begin building at the site Pierre Laclede chose on the west bank of the Mississippi: the founding of St. Louis.
Cyrus McCormick is born in Virginia. He patented his mechanical reaper in 1834; his company became part of International Harvester in 1902.
The battleship USS Maine explodes in Havana harbor, killing 261 of her crew. 'Remember the Maine!' becomes the cry for war with Spain.
The nation's first 911 emergency telephone system goes into service in Haleyville, Alabama.
CBBS, the first computer bulletin board system, goes online in Chicago. Ward Christensen and Randy Suess started it while snowed in by the Great Blizzard of 1978.
Off Charleston, the Confederate submarine H.L. Hunley sinks USS Housatonic: the first submarine to sink a warship. The Hunley and her eight men never returned.
Volkswagen builds Beetle number 15,007,034, passing the Ford Model T as the most-produced car in history.
Elm Farm Ollie, a Guernsey from Bismarck, Missouri, becomes the first cow to fly and be milked in flight, aboard a Ford Trimotor. The milk is parachuted down over St. Louis.
At Lowell Observatory in Arizona, Clyde Tombaugh, 23 and raised on a Kansas farm, discovers Pluto by comparing photographs of the sky taken days apart.
U.S. Marines land on Iwo Jima. The battle lasted five weeks and cost about 6,800 American lives.
John Glenn orbits the Earth three times in Friendship 7, the first American to do so. His Mercury capsule was built by McDonnell Aircraft in St. Louis.
In Wales, Richard Trevithick's steam locomotive hauls 10 tons of iron and 70 men nearly ten miles from Penydarren: the world's first locomotive-hauled railway journey.
The first telephone directory is issued in New Haven, Connecticut: one sheet of cardboard with 50 names and no numbers.
The first Daytona 500 ends in a photo finish. Three days later, after studying photographs and newsreels, NASCAR declares Lee Petty the winner over Johnny Beauchamp.
President Coolidge signs the Radio Act of 1927, creating the Federal Radio Commission to license broadcasters, hams and ship stations. The FCC replaced it in 1934.
Marines raise the U.S. flag on Mount Suribachi, Iwo Jima. Joe Rosenthal's photograph of the second raising that day won the Pulitzer Prize.
Steve Jobs, co-founder of Apple, is born in San Francisco.
USS Ranger is launched at Newport News, Virginia, christened by First Lady Lou Henry Hoover: the first U.S. ship designed and built from the keel up as an aircraft carrier.
At Daventry, England, Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins detect a bomber by radio waves reflected from a BBC shortwave transmitter: the experiment that launched British radar.
In the Battle of the Java Sea, a Japanese force defeats an Allied squadron under Dutch Rear Adm. Karel Doorman, who is lost with his flagship De Ruyter.
Maryland charters the Baltimore and Ohio Rail Road, which became the first steam-operated common-carrier railroad in the United States.
Stranded on Jamaica, Columbus uses an almanac's prediction of that evening's lunar eclipse to frighten the islanders into feeding his crew again.
Over Jefferson Barracks near St. Louis, Albert Berry jumps from a Benoist biplane at 1,500 feet: the first documented parachute jump from a powered airplane.
The B-50 bomber Lucky Lady II lands at Fort Worth, Texas, after 94 hours and four refuelings in the air: the first airplane to circle the world nonstop.
Alexander Graham Bell is born in Edinburgh, Scotland.
Nine motor clubs with 1,500 members meet in Chicago and form the American Automobile Association, to press for roads fit for cars.
At Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, with President Truman in the audience, Winston Churchill says 'an Iron Curtain has descended across the Continent.'
The Homebrew Computer Club meets for the first time, in Gordon French's garage in Menlo Park, California. Steve Wozniak said it inspired him to design the Apple I.
The Supreme Court rules 7 to 2 against Dred Scott, who had first sued for his freedom at the Old Courthouse in St. Louis in 1846, holding that he could not be a citizen.
Soldiers of the U.S. 9th Armored Division capture the Ludendorff Bridge at Remagen intact and cross the Rhine. The bridge collapsed ten days later.
Daytona Beach holds its first stock car race, on a 3.2-mile course of beach and road. The sandy turns become nearly impassable and the race is stopped three laps early.
At Hampton Roads, Virginia, USS Monitor and CSS Virginia fight for hours at close range to a draw: the first battle between ironclad warships.
Three Flags Day: in St. Louis the Spanish flag came down on March 9, the French flag flew for a day, and now the American flag goes up. Upper Louisiana joins the United States.
In Boston, Alexander Graham Bell speaks the first words heard clearly over a telephone: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'
The Great Blizzard of 1888 begins. Over four days it buries the Northeast under as much as 58 inches of snow and kills about 400. New York later moved its wires underground.
Eight days after taking office, President Roosevelt explains the banking crisis to the nation by radio: the first 'fireside chat'.
At CERN, Tim Berners-Lee hands in 'Information Management: A Proposal', the plan that became the World Wide Web.
From his back garden in Bath, England, William Herschel spots Uranus with a telescope he built himself. He first took it for a comet.
Eli Whitney is granted his patent for the cotton gin.
Casey Jones is born in southeastern Missouri (his family Bible says 1863). The Illinois Central engineer died at the throttle of No. 382 in 1900, the only person killed in the wreck.
Symbolics.com is registered: the first .com domain name on the internet.
At Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert Goddard launches the first liquid-fueled rocket. It rises 41 feet, flies for 2.5 seconds and lands in a cabbage field.
The nuclear submarine USS Skate becomes the first submarine to surface at the North Pole. Her crew scatters the ashes of polar explorer Sir Hubert Wilkins there.
The Tri-State Tornado touches down in Shannon County, Missouri, and runs 219 miles across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana. It kills at least 695, the deadliest tornado in U.S. history.
The Standard Time Act puts the railroads' time zones into federal law, with the Interstate Commerce Commission to draw the lines, and adds daylight saving time.
At the railway station in Terowie, South Australia, Gen. Douglas MacArthur, just out of the Philippines, tells reporters: 'I came through and I shall return.'
St. Louis native Jack Dorsey sends the first tweet: 'just setting up my twttr'.
Intel introduces the Pentium processor: 3.1 million transistors, running at 60 MHz.
Lewis and Clark leave Fort Clatsop on the Pacific coast and start for home. They reached St. Louis six months later, on September 23.
Gus Grissom and John Young fly Gemini 3, the first crewed Gemini, in a spacecraft built by McDonnell in St. Louis. Young smuggles a corned beef sandwich aboard.
The Great Escape: 76 Allied airmen crawl out of Stalag Luft III through the tunnel 'Harry'. Three reached home; 50 of those recaptured were shot on Hitler's order.
Just after midnight the tanker Exxon Valdez strikes Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska, and spills more than 10 million gallons of crude oil.
In Wales, the Swansea and Mumbles Railway begins carrying fare-paying passengers in horse-drawn carriages: the world's first passenger railway service.
Norman Borlaug is born on a farm in Saude, Iowa. His high-yield, disease-resistant wheat led the Green Revolution and won him the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize.
The spinach growers of Crystal City, Texas, have a statue of Popeye standing in town, in thanks for what the sailor did for sales of their crop.
Marconi sends a wireless message across the English Channel, from Wimereux, France, to the South Foreland Lighthouse in England.
On the Etang de Berre in France, Henri Fabre takes off from the water in his Hydravion: the first seaplane flight. The longest of four hops that day is about 600 meters.
An ice jam upstream stops Niagara Falls. For about 40 hours almost no water goes over; waterwheels stop and the mills shut down.
Jethro Tull is baptised at Basildon, England. His horse-drawn seed drill of 1701 sowed seed in neat rows at an even depth, in place of scattering it by hand.
At the Harland and Wolff yard in Belfast, the keel of the Titanic is laid. She was launched on May 31, 1911, and sank on April 15, 1912.
TIROS-1, the first weather satellite, is launched from Cape Canaveral. In two and a half months it sends back 23,000 pictures of the Earth, 19,000 of them usable for weather analysis.
Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne found the Apple Computer Company as a partnership in Los Altos, California.
Walter Chrysler is born in Wamego, Kansas. He spent years as a roundhouse mechanic on Western railroads before turning to cars, and founded the Chrysler Corporation in 1925.
The first Pony Express rider leaves St. Joseph, Missouri, for Sacramento, about 1,900 miles away. Mail crossed in some 10 days; the telegraph ended the service after 18 months.
On a Manhattan sidewalk, Motorola's Martin Cooper makes the first call from a handheld cell phone, a 2.5-pound prototype. He calls his rival at AT&T.
Bill Gates and Paul Allen found Microsoft in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to sell their BASIC for the Altair 8800.
An F5 tornado strikes Tupelo, Mississippi, killing more than 200 people. Among the survivors is one-year-old Elvis Presley.
Early Bird (Intelsat I) is launched: the first commercial communications satellite in geosynchronous orbit, carrying television and telephone calls across the Atlantic.
U.S. carrier planes sink the Japanese battleship Yamato, the heaviest ever built, south of Kyushu with at least 11 torpedoes and 6 bombs. About 3,055 of her 3,332 men are lost.
IBM announces the System/360: a whole family of computers, small to large, that all run the same programs.
Mary Hawes of Burroughs gathers computer makers, users and academics, Grace Hopper among them, at the University of Pennsylvania to plan a common business language. It became COBOL.
Maj. Gen. Edward King surrenders the U.S. and Filipino force on Bataan. Some 75,000 prisoners are driven north on the 65-mile Bataan Death March.
Nebraska keeps the first Arbor Day, the idea of J. Sterling Morton of Nebraska City. An estimated one million trees are planted across the state.
Shortly after noon the new liner Titanic leaves Southampton, England, on her maiden voyage to New York.
Apollo 13 lifts off for the Moon. Two days out an oxygen tank explodes: 'Houston, we've had a problem.' Lovell, Swigert and Haise got home safely on April 17.
President Roosevelt dies and Harry Truman of Independence, Missouri, vice president for 82 days, is sworn in. He said it felt 'like the moon, the stars, and all the planets had fallen on me.'
Yuri Gagarin orbits the Earth once in Vostok 1, a flight of 108 minutes: the first human in space. Twenty years later to the day, Space Shuttle Columbia made the first shuttle flight.
George Westinghouse is granted U.S. patent 88,929 for the railway air brake. Today's train brakes still descend from his design.
Black Sunday: one of the worst dust storms in American history rolls over the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles. A reporter's story on it gave the region its name: the Dust Bowl.
At a broadcasters' convention in Chicago, Ampex demonstrates its videotape recorder, replaying a speech moments after it ended. It took $2 million in orders in four days.
The Titanic sinks at 2:20 a.m., two hours and forty minutes after striking an iceberg. Of more than 2,200 aboard, about 1,500 die; the Carpathia rescues 710.
Wilbur Wright is born near Millville, Indiana, four years before his brother Orville.
Ford introduces the Mustang at the New York World's Fair, priced from $2,368. Dealers take 22,000 orders the first day.
Lt. Col. Jimmy Doolittle leads 16 B-25 bombers off the carrier USS Hornet to bomb Tokyo and other cities. None of the planes could return to the ship; most crews came down in China.
Electronics magazine publishes Gordon Moore's article observing that the number of components on a chip doubles about every year: Moore's Law.
Apollo 16's lunar module Orion lands on the Moon with John Young and Charles Duke.
Manfred von Richthofen, the 'Red Baron', is shot down and killed over France. He was credited with 80 victories; historians think ground fire, not another pilot, brought him down.
The first railroad bridge across the Mississippi opens at Rock Island, Illinois. Two weeks later a steamboat hit it, and the railroads hired Abraham Lincoln to defend the bridge in court.
At noon about 50,000 settlers race into Oklahoma to claim two million acres. By sundown Guthrie and Oklahoma City each hold some 10,000 people.
Brunel's Great Western, the first steamship built for the Atlantic, reaches New York after 15 days. The smaller Sirius, which left four days earlier, beat her in by one day.
Space Shuttle Discovery carries the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit. Its mirror proved to be ground to the wrong shape; astronauts fitted corrective optics in December 1993.
Elbe Day: American and Soviet soldiers meet at the Elbe River near Torgau, cutting Germany in two.
The converted tanker Ideal X leaves Port Newark, New Jersey, for Houston carrying 58 containers, with 58 trucks waiting at the other end: the first successful container ship.
The Baltimore and Ohio's Royal Blue makes its last run between Washington and Jersey City. In 1895 a Royal Blue train was the first in America hauled by an electric locomotive.
Samuel Morse is born in Charlestown, Massachusetts. He made his name as a portrait painter before the telegraph.
The steamboat Sultana, of the St. Louis to New Orleans run, explodes on the Mississippi above Memphis with 2,127 aboard, most of them freed Union prisoners. Some 1,164 die.
Fletcher Christian leads the mutiny on HMS Bounty. Captain Bligh and 18 loyal men are set adrift in an open boat, which Bligh sails more than 3,500 nautical miles to Timor.
Eli Janney of Alexandria, Virginia, is granted U.S. patent 138,405 for his knuckle coupler, which let cars couple without a man standing between them.
The last Oldsmobile, an Alero signed by the assembly-line workers, leaves the plant in Lansing, Michigan, ending a name that began in 1897.
Casey Jones dies at Vaughan, Mississippi, braking his Illinois Central passenger train to the last before it hits a stalled freight. He is the only one killed.
The Louisiana Purchase Exposition, the St. Louis World's Fair, opens in Forest Park. President Theodore Roosevelt starts it by telegraph from the White House.
Amtrak runs its first trains, taking over intercity passenger service from 20 railroads. Of 366 train routes running the day before, it keeps 184.
The United States switches off 'Selective Availability', the deliberate blurring of the civilian GPS signal. Receivers go from about 100 meters of error to about 5.
A Digital Equipment marketer sends an ad for a computer demonstration to about 400 ARPANET users at once: the first spam e-mail. He is made to promise not to do it again.
A U.S. Army lieutenant is handed the keys to the French canal works in Panama, and the American effort begins. The Panama Canal opened to ships on August 15, 1914.
Alan Shepard rides Freedom 7, a Mercury capsule built by McDonnell Aircraft, 116 miles up on a 15-minute flight: the first American in space.
The airship Hindenburg burns while landing at Lakehurst, New Jersey. Of 97 aboard, 35 die, and one man on the ground. Radio reporter Herbert Morrison's recording carries the words 'Oh, the humanity.'
Queen Elizabeth II and President Mitterrand open the Channel Tunnel: 31 miles of railway between England and France, 23.5 of them under the sea.
In St. Petersburg, Alexander Popov presents his lightning detector, a receiver that rings a bell when it picks up the radio pulse of a distant strike. Russia keeps May 7 as Radio Day.
The German submarine U-20 torpedoes the liner Lusitania off the Old Head of Kinsale, Ireland. She sinks in 18 minutes; 1,197 of the 1,960 aboard die, about 128 of them Americans.
The Smith-Lever Act creates the Cooperative Extension Service, sending the land-grant colleges' know-how out to farm families.
V-E Day: Germany's surrender takes effect and the war in Europe is over. It is President Truman's 61st birthday; he was born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884.
British escorts force the submarine U-110 to the surface, and a boarding party from HMS Bulldog carries off her Enigma machine and code books. The capture is kept secret.
At Promontory Summit, Utah, Leland Stanford drives the last spike joining the Central Pacific and Union Pacific. The telegraph flashes one word across the country: DONE.
A dust storm that rose off the Great Plains two days earlier reaches New York, Boston and Washington. On the way it dropped 12 million pounds of dust on Chicago.
In New York, IBM's Deep Blue wins the sixth game and the match, 3.5 to 2.5: the first time a computer beats a reigning world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match.
In Berlin, Konrad Zuse presents the Z3, built from 2,600 relays: the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer. Bombing destroyed it in 1943.
The first Formula One world championship race is run at Silverstone, England, with King George VI watching. Nino Farina wins in an Alfa Romeo.
William Clark and about 30 men set out from Camp Dubois, Illinois, and start up the Missouri River: the Lewis and Clark Expedition is under way.
President Lincoln signs the law creating the U.S. Department of Agriculture. He called it 'the people's department.'
The Dambusters: 19 Lancasters of No. 617 Squadron under Guy Gibson fly to Germany with Barnes Wallis's bouncing bombs and breach the Mohne and Eder dams. Eight aircraft do not return.
A college baseball game in New York, Columbia against Princeton, is the first sporting event shown on television in the United States.
Jacqueline Cochran, flying a Canadair Sabre over Rogers Dry Lake, California, becomes the first woman to break the sound barrier. Chuck Yeager had encouraged her.
New England's Dark Day: the sky goes so dark that candles are needed from noon. Forest-fire smoke, fog and cloud were to blame; many feared the Day of Judgment.
Charles Lindbergh takes off from New York in the Spirit of St. Louis, paid for by St. Louis backers. He lands in Paris the next day, 3,600 miles and more than 33 hours later.
Amelia Earhart lands her Lockheed Vega near Derry, Northern Ireland, 14 hours 56 minutes out of Newfoundland: the first woman to fly the Atlantic alone.
Abraham Lincoln is granted U.S. patent 6,469 for inflatable bladders to float a steamboat over shoals. He is the only president to hold a patent.
Microsoft releases Windows 3.0, the first version of Windows to win wide acclaim. It sold about 10 million copies.
The submarine USS Squalus sinks on a test dive off New Hampshire in 243 feet of water. Twenty-six men die; divers bring up all 33 survivors with the new McCann rescue chamber.
Samuel Morse opens his telegraph line with a message from Washington to Baltimore: 'What hath God wrought.'
President Kennedy asks Congress to commit the nation to 'landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth' before the decade is out.
Henry Ford and his son Edsel drive the 15-millionth Model T out of the factory, and the car's long run comes to an end.
Operation Dynamo begins at Dunkirk. By June 4 a fleet of more than 800 vessels, many of them small civilian boats, has brought 338,226 Allied soldiers back across the Channel.
About 6:30 p.m. a tornado cuts a mile-wide path through St. Louis, crosses the Mississippi at the Eads Bridge and strikes East St. Louis. At least 255 people are killed.
The German battleship Bismarck is sunk in the Atlantic by the Royal Navy, three days after she sank HMS Hood. Of more than 2,200 men aboard, 114 survive.
Volkswagen is founded in Berlin by the German Labour Front. The name means 'people's car.'
In fog on the St. Lawrence River the liner Empress of Ireland is rammed by the collier Storstad and sinks in 14 minutes. Of 1,477 aboard, 1,012 die.
Ray Harroun wins the first Indianapolis 500 in the Marmon Wasp at 74.6 miles per hour. He drives alone, with a rear-view mirror in place of a riding mechanic.
After a day of heavy rain the South Fork Dam gives way above Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The flood kills 2,208. Clara Barton's Red Cross stays more than five months.
At 6 p.m. Eastern, Ted Turner's Cable News Network signs on from Atlanta: the first television channel to carry news 24 hours a day.
Guglielmo Marconi, 22, applies for British patent 12039. It becomes the first patent for a communication system based on radio waves.
Surveyor 1 sets down in the Ocean of Storms: the first American spacecraft to soft-land on another world, four months after the Soviet Luna 9. It sends back 11,237 photographs.
Ed White leaves Gemini 4 for 36 minutes, steering with a hand-held oxygen jet: the first American to walk in space. Coming back in, he calls it 'the saddest moment of my life.'
Congress renames the Louisiana Territory the Missouri Territory, to avoid confusion with the new state of Louisiana. St. Louis is its capital; Missouri becomes a state in 1821.
In Detroit, Henry Ford takes his Quadricycle out for its first drive: a 4-horsepower, two-cylinder engine on four bicycle wheels, good for 20 mph.
Battle of Midway: six months after Pearl Harbor, American planes fatally hit the Japanese carriers Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu in a single day. The U.S. loses the carrier Yorktown.
Ada Lovelace, 17, meets Charles Babbage through her tutor, Mary Somerville. Later in the month he invites her to see the prototype of his difference engine.
Richard Hollingshead opens the first drive-in movie theater, with room for 400 cars, at Pennsauken, New Jersey. His slogan: the whole family is welcome, however noisy the children.
D-Day: 156,000 Allied soldiers land on five Normandy beaches - Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword - from nearly 7,000 vessels. It is the largest seaborne invasion in history.
The Edmund Fitzgerald is launched sideways at River Rouge, Michigan, before more than 15,000 people. At 729 feet she is the largest ship on the Great Lakes. The champagne bottle takes three tries.
An F5 tornado crosses Burnett's Mound, which legend said would shield the city, and cuts 22 miles through Topeka, Kansas, destroying 820 homes: the costliest U.S. tornado to that time.
Storms stall over the Black Hills of South Dakota and drop 15 inches of rain in about six hours. Rapid Creek floods Rapid City overnight; 238 people die.
The Great Northern Railway inaugurates the Empire Builder, named for its founder, James J. Hill. Amtrak still runs the train every day between Chicago and Seattle or Portland.
The first Apple II computers go on sale. Designed by Steve Wozniak around a 6502 processor, with color graphics, it costs $1,298 with 4 KB of memory.
The Paris-Bordeaux-Paris race starts: 732 miles. Emile Levassor drives the whole way himself in 48 hours 48 minutes, about 15 mph, but his two-seater is ineligible for first prize.
Bryan Allen pedals the Gossamer Albatross, a 70-pound aircraft designed by Paul MacCready's team, 22 miles across the English Channel in 2 hours 49 minutes on leg power alone.
A week after D-Day, Germany launches its first V-1 flying bombs against London. The Allies call them buzz bombs or doodlebugs; 10,492 will be launched at Britain.
Pioneer 10, launched in 1972, crosses the orbit of Neptune: the first human-made object to pass beyond the orbits of the major planets. Its last signal is received in 2003.
The Census Bureau dedicates the first UNIVAC I, designed principally by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. It has 6,103 vacuum tubes and weighs 16,686 pounds; 46 are built.
The New York Central's 20th Century Limited makes its first run, New York to Chicago in 20 hours. Passengers board along a crimson carpet: the origin of 'red-carpet treatment.'
The excursion steamer General Slocum catches fire in New York's East River with a church picnic aboard. Rotten life preservers and fire hose fail; an estimated 1,021 of 1,342 aboard die.
Ford Motor Company is incorporated in Detroit with $28,000 in cash from twelve investors.
Valentina Tereshkova, a textile worker and amateur parachutist, is launched in Vostok 6: the first woman in space. She makes 48 orbits in a flight of 70.8 hours.
Battle of Boonville: Nathaniel Lyon's Union troops, brought up the Missouri River by steamboat, scatter the Missouri State Guard in about 20 minutes. Federal control of the river is never broken.
Challenger lifts off on STS-7 with mission specialist Sally Ride aboard: the first American woman in space. The crew of five is the largest yet flown in one spacecraft.
President Roosevelt signs the Communications Act of 1934, replacing the Federal Radio Commission with the Federal Communications Commission.
Samuel Morse is issued U.S. patent 1,647, 'Telegraph Signs', for communicating information by signals by the application of electro-magnetism.
CBS airs the first 'Toast of the Town', hosted by Ed Sullivan. Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis perform; Rodgers and Hammerstein preview South Pacific. The show runs until 1971.
In Manchester, England, the 'Baby' runs its first program: 17 instructions and 52 minutes to find the highest proper divisor of 262,144. It is the first electronic stored-program computer.
Mike Melvill flies SpaceShipOne, built by Burt Rutan's Scaled Composites, from Mojave, California, to 328,491 feet: the first privately funded human spaceflight.
Near Hammond, Indiana, an empty troop train whose engineer has fallen asleep rams the Hagenbeck-Wallace Circus train at about 4 a.m. The wooden cars burn; 86 die and 127 are hurt.
Germany invades the Soviet Union: more than 3.8 million Axis troops on an 1,800-mile front. Operation Barbarossa becomes the largest and costliest military offensive in history.
Alan Turing is born in Maida Vale, London. He finishes his paper 'On Computable Numbers' in 1936; in the war he leads Hut 8 at Bletchley Park, the section working on German naval codes.
A British Airways 747 flies into ash from the volcano Galunggung, south of Java, and all four engines stop. The crew glides down from 37,000 feet, restarts them and lands at Jakarta. All 263 survive.
Lucien B. Smith of Kent, Ohio, is issued U.S. patent 66,182, 'Wire fence': the first American patent for barbed wire. Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, patents the modern kind in 1874.
CBS airs the variety special 'Premiere' in color over five East Coast stations. Black-and-white sets cannot show it and only a few dozen color sets exist; CBS drops its system in October.
Queen Elizabeth II and President Eisenhower formally open the St. Lawrence Seaway at Saint-Lambert, Quebec. Its 15 locks let ocean ships sail from the Atlantic into the Great Lakes.
At 8:01 a.m. in a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a 10-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum, 67 cents, becomes the first product rung up at a checkout by scanning its UPC bar code.
Joshua Slocum sails the 37-foot sloop Spray into Newport, Rhode Island, three years and more than 46,000 miles after leaving Boston: the first person to sail around the world alone.
Hurricane Audrey comes ashore near the Texas-Louisiana line with 125 mph winds and a surge of up to 12 feet. At least 416 people die, 371 of them in and around Cameron, Louisiana.
Barclays Bank in Enfield, London, installs the world's first cash machine, invented by John Shepherd-Barron. Customers feed it a paper voucher and a PIN; the limit is 10 pounds.
Benz & Cie. and Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft formally merge as Daimler-Benz AG, two years after agreeing to work together. Their cars will carry the name Mercedes-Benz.
President Eisenhower signs the Federal-Aid Highway Act: 41,000 miles of Interstate highways, $25 billion over 10 years, 90 percent federally paid. No American public works project had been larger.
The first iPhone goes on sale in the United States, announced that January: $499 with 4 GB or $599 with 8 GB, on a two-year AT&T contract. 270,000 are sold in the first week.
A meteor explodes in the air over Tunguska in Siberia, flattening about 830 square miles of forest. June 30 is now kept as Asteroid Day.
The first production Corvettes are built by hand in an old truck plant in Flint, Michigan: 300 that year, all white with red interiors and fiberglass bodies. In 1954 production moves to St. Louis.
President Lincoln signs the Pacific Railway Act, authorizing the Union Pacific and Central Pacific to build a railroad from the Missouri River at Council Bluffs, Iowa, to Sacramento, California.
The radiotelegraph convention signed in 1906 takes effect, making SOS - three dots, three dashes, three dots - the distress signal for ships at sea. Germany has used it since 1905.
At 2:30 p.m., before a Dodgers-Phillies game, New York station WNBT shows a clock face marked 'Bulova Watch Time' for one minute: the first paid television advertisement in the United States.
President Lincoln signs the Morrill Act. Each state gets 30,000 acres of public land per member of Congress to fund colleges teaching agriculture and the mechanic arts: the land-grant colleges.
Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan take off from Lae, New Guinea, in a Lockheed Electra for Howland Island, 2,556 miles away. They never arrive. She is declared dead in 1939.
Karl Benz takes his three-wheeled motor car on a trip around Mannheim, reported in the local paper: the first public outing of the Patent-Motorwagen. Its engine makes about one horsepower.
On Stoke Bank, south of Grantham, England, driver Joseph Duddington takes Nigel Gresley's locomotive Mallard to 126 mph. No steam locomotive has officially gone faster.
Charles Carroll of Carrollton, almost 91 and the last living signer of the Declaration of Independence, lays the first stone of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. It is his last public act.
President Grant dedicates the Eads Bridge at St. Louis, seven years in the building. James Eads' 520-foot center arch is the longest rigid span yet built, and it pioneers the use of steel.
Mars Pathfinder lands on airbags in Ares Vallis, carrying the 23-pound rover Sojourner: the first rover to operate beyond the Earth and Moon. Its last data arrives on September 27.
Germany opens Operation Citadel against the Soviet lines around Kursk: 2,928 German tanks against 5,128 Soviet. The fighting lasts until August 23: the deadliest armored battle in history.
Jeff Bezos incorporates Cadabra, Inc., in Washington state, working from the garage of his house in Bellevue. As Amazon it opens for business as an online bookseller on July 16, 1995.
The British airship R34 reaches Mineola, Long Island, 108 hours out of East Fortune, Scotland, with only a few gallons of fuel left: the first east-to-west crossing of the Atlantic by air.
The Chillicothe Baking Company of Chillicothe, Missouri, sells the first sliced bread, cut on Otto Rohwedder's machine. Its ads call it the greatest forward step in baking since bread was wrapped.
On her maiden voyage the liner United States crosses the Atlantic in 3 days, 10 hours, 40 minutes at 35.59 knots, beating by more than 10 hours the record Queen Mary had held for 14 years.
Atlantis lifts off at 11:29 a.m. Eastern with a crew of four on STS-135, the 135th and final mission of the Space Shuttle program. She lands on July 21.
About 7:20 a.m. two Nashville, Chattanooga and St. Louis passenger trains collide at Dutchman's Curve in Nashville. 101 die and at least 171 are hurt: the worst rail accident in U.S. history.
Furnace Creek in Death Valley, California, records 134 degrees Fahrenheit: still the highest temperature on record anywhere in the world, though some meteorologists doubt the reading.
The date Britain counts as the start of the Battle of Britain, which runs to October 31: the first major military campaign fought entirely by air forces. In July the Luftwaffe hits coastal convoys.
Telstar 1, built by Bell Labs for AT&T, is launched from Cape Canaveral: a 170-pound sphere 35 inches across. On July 23 it relays the first live television signal across the Atlantic.
Skylab, launched in 1973 and home to three crews, falls to Earth, scattering debris across the Indian Ocean and Western Australia. The Shire of Esperance fines NASA A$400 for littering.
President Biden unveils the first image from the James Webb Space Telescope: the galaxy cluster SMACS 0723 as it was 4.6 billion years ago, seen with a 6.5-meter mirror of 18 gold-coated segments.
Five days of extreme heat begin in Chicago. Midway Airport reaches 106 degrees on July 13, and 739 heat-related deaths are counted in the city.
Live Aid: concerts at Wembley Stadium in London and JFK Stadium in Philadelphia are linked by satellite for 16 hours. An estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 nations watch on television.
Mariner 4 flies past Mars, 6,118 miles up, and stores 21 pictures on its tape recorder: the first images of another planet returned from deep space. Each takes about six hours to send home.
Nintendo releases the Family Computer in Japan for 14,800 yen, with Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr. and Popeye. Designed by Masayuki Uemura, it reaches America two years later as the NES.
The world's first parking meter is installed in Oklahoma City. Newspaper publisher Carl Magee asked for the design; two Oklahoma State engineering professors, Thuesen and Hale, worked it out.
At 5:29 a.m. in the Jornada del Muerto desert of New Mexico, the 'gadget' explodes on a 100-foot steel tower with the force of 25 kilotons of TNT. Trinity is the first detonation of a nuclear weapon.
At 10:18 p.m. munitions being loaded on the cargo ship E. A. Bryan explode at Port Chicago, California. 320 die, 202 of them African-American. Fifty men are later convicted of mutiny.
At 7:05 p.m. two walkways in the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City, Missouri, fall onto a tea dance in the lobby. 114 die and 216 are hurt. A change to the hanger rods had doubled the load on the beams.
Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce, backed by Arthur Rock, found NM Electronics in Mountain View, California. It becomes Intel, for Integrated Electronics. Its first product is a 64-bit memory chip.
Prince Albert attends the float-out at Bristol of Brunel's Great Britain, 322 feet long, the largest vessel yet built and the first large ocean-going ship with an iron hull and a screw propeller.
The lunar module Eagle lands in the Sea of Tranquility. Hours later Neil Armstrong steps onto the Moon: 'one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind.' Some 600 million people watch.
Viking 1 lands in Chryse Planitia: the first successful Mars lander. Planned for July 4, the landing waited while a smoother site was found. The lander works until November 1982.
Vostok Station, 11,444 feet up on the Antarctic ice, records minus 128.6 degrees Fahrenheit: the lowest natural temperature ever reliably measured on Earth.
Wiley Post returns to Floyd Bennett Field, New York, after 7 days, 18 hours, 49 minutes: the first to fly around the world alone, with an autopilot in place of a navigator. 50,000 people greet him.
Mariner 1, bound for Venus, veers off course and is destroyed 293 seconds after launch. A missing overline in the guidance equations costs $18.5 million: 'the most expensive hyphen in history.'
Chicago dentist Ernest Pfennig becomes the first owner of a Ford: a two-cylinder, 8-horsepower Model A, base price $750. Ford Motor Company has $223.65 left in the bank.
Commodore introduces the Amiga at Lincoln Center in New York, with Andy Warhol and Debbie Harry on hand: a 68000 processor, 256 KB of memory, 4,096 colors and preemptive multitasking.
The steamer Eastland, with 2,500 aboard for a Western Electric company picnic, rolls over at her dock in the Chicago River. 844 die: the largest loss of life from a shipwreck on the Great Lakes.
Apollo 11 splashes down in the Pacific after 8 days, 3 hours and 18 minutes, and the carrier USS Hornet picks up the crew. They bring home 47.5 pounds of the Moon.
About 11:10 p.m., in thick fog off Nantucket, the Swedish liner Stockholm hits the Italian liner Andrea Doria. 51 die; 1,660 of the 1,706 aboard Andrea Doria are saved before she sinks at 10:09 a.m.
NASA launches Syncom 2, built by Hughes Aircraft: the world's first geosynchronous communications satellite. In August it carries a call between President Kennedy and Nigeria's prime minister.
The steamship Great Eastern reaches Heart's Content, Newfoundland, in thick fog, and the Atlantic cable goes into service. It sends 8 words a minute. The 1858 cable had lasted three weeks.
John Cunningham takes the de Havilland Comet up from Hatfield, England, on its first flight: the world's first commercial jet airliner, with four Ghost turbojets in its wing roots.
At 9:40 a.m., in thick fog, an Army B-25 bomber hits the Empire State Building between the 78th and 80th floors. 14 die. Elevator operator Betty Lou Oliver survives a 75-story fall.
President Eisenhower signs the National Aeronautics and Space Act, close on the heels of Sputnik. It creates NASA, which takes over the work of the old NACA on October 1.
Fifteen minutes after midnight the submarine I-58 torpedoes the cruiser Indianapolis, which has just delivered atomic bomb parts to Tinian. She sinks in 12 minutes. Of 1,195 men, 316 survive.
At 9:05 a.m. the Volkswagen plant at Puebla, Mexico, builds the last original Beetle. 21,529,464 were made in all.
On Apollo 15, David Scott and Jim Irwin take the first drive on the Moon. The Boeing-built Lunar Roving Vehicle weighs 460 pounds and runs on two silver-zinc batteries. It covers 17.25 miles.
Up to 7.5 inches of rain in an hour sends a flood down Colorado's Big Thompson Canyon, cresting at 30 feet. At least 144 die, the day before the 100th anniversary of Colorado statehood.
At 12:01 a.m. MTV goes on the air over film of the first landing on the Moon. Its first music video is 'Video Killed the Radio Star' by the Buggles.
The Mississippi crests at St. Louis at a record 49.6 feet, nearly 20 feet above flood stage. The 52-foot floodwall holds with just over two feet to spare. The river stays in flood until October 7.

Andrew Hallidie's Clay Street Hill Railroad makes its first run in San Francisco, a day later than its franchise required: the first successful cable-hauled street railway. Service starts September 1.
About 2:27 a.m. the Japanese destroyer Amagiri cuts PT-109 in two in the Solomon Islands. Two men die. Lt. John F. Kennedy and ten others swim 3.5 miles to a deserted island; rescue comes August 8.
At 11:15 p.m. Eastern the nuclear submarine Nautilus, Commander William Anderson, passes under the North Pole: the first vessel to reach it. She crosses beneath the ice in 96 hours.
Radio Shack announces the TRS-80 at a New York press conference: a Z80 computer for $399, or $599 with a 12-inch monitor and a tape recorder. More than 10,000 sell in the first month and a half.
On Alexander Hamilton's advice Congress creates the Revenue-Marine: ten cutters to enforce the customs laws. Until 1798 it is the nation's only armed force afloat. In 1915 it becomes the Coast Guard.
Agamemnon lands the eastern end of the first Atlantic telegraph cable at Valentia Island, Ireland; Niagara lands the western end at Trinity Bay, Newfoundland, that morning. It fails in September.
At 8:15 a.m. the B-29 Enola Gay, flown from Tinian by Col. Paul Tibbets, drops the atomic bomb 'Little Boy' on Hiroshima. By the end of the year 90,000 to 166,000 people there are dead.
Tim Berners-Lee of CERN posts a short summary of his World Wide Web project to the newsgroup alt.hypertext, inviting collaborators. The first website has been up since December.
IBM gives Harvard its Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator: Howard Aiken's Mark I, 51 feet long, 765,000 parts, 500 miles of wire. It adds three times a second. Grace Hopper helps program it.
Thor Heyerdahl's balsa raft Kon-Tiki smashes onto the reef at Raroia in the Tuamotus, 101 days and 4,300 miles out of Callao, Peru, with a crew of six.
At Honesdale, Pennsylvania, Horatio Allen drives the English-built Stourbridge Lion on its first run: the first locomotive operated in the United States. It proves too heavy for the track.
The DeWitt Clinton makes its first passenger run on the Mohawk and Hudson Railroad, Albany to Schenectady, in 38 minutes: the first working steam locomotive built for service in New York state.
At 11:02 a.m. the B-29 Bockscar, Maj. Charles Sweeney, drops the atomic bomb 'Fat Man' on Nagasaki; the first target, Kokura, was passed over. 60,000 to 80,000 people die by the end of the year.
Missouri is admitted to the Union as the 24th state, a slave state under the Missouri Compromise. The temporary capital is St. Charles; Jefferson City takes over in 1826.
Alexander Graham Bell hears voices sent eight miles over the telegraph line from Brantford to Paris, Ontario. It works only one way, but many sources call it the world's first long-distance call.
Actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil receive U.S. patent 2,292,387 for a radio torpedo guidance system that hops between frequencies to defeat jamming. The Navy turns it down.
The Fifteen Guinea Special runs from Liverpool to Carlisle and back behind four engines in turn: British Rail's last main-line passenger train hauled by steam. The steam ban starts the next day.
IBM releases the Personal Computer, model 5150, developed in Boca Raton, Florida: an Intel 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 16 KB of memory and PC DOS from Microsoft, starting at $1,565.
Eagle Day: the Luftwaffe opens its all-out assault on the Royal Air Force. Germany loses 47 or 48 aircraft; the RAF loses 13 fighters and 11 bombers in the air and 47 planes on the ground.
Seven motorcycle races are the first motor racing at Carl Fisher's new Indianapolis Motor Speedway. Car racing follows within days on crushed stone; soon the track is repaved with 3.2 million bricks.
At 7 p.m. in Washington, President Truman announces that Japan has surrendered. The largest crowd in the history of Times Square gathers. The surrender is signed on USS Missouri on September 2.
Just after 4:10 p.m. Eastern a blackout spreads over eight states and Ontario: 55 million people. A power line touched a tree in Ohio, and a software bug had stalled the control room's alarm system.
Near Strasburg, Colorado, the Kansas Pacific drives the last spike of the first continuous transcontinental railroad. It is the only all-rail route across the country until 1872.
The Panama Canal is formally opened as the steamship Ancon makes the passage. The 51-mile waterway cost the United States almost $500 million and about 5,600 workers' lives.
Ohio State's Big Ear radio telescope records a strong 72-second signal at 1420 MHz from the direction of Sagittarius. Days later Jerry Ehman writes 'Wow!' on the printout. It has never recurred.
Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchange greetings over the new Atlantic cable. Her message runs 98 words. The next morning New York fires a 100-gun salute; that night the city is lit up.
Air Force Capt. Joseph Kittinger steps from a balloon gondola at 102,800 feet, falls for 4 minutes 36 seconds and reaches 614 mph. His jump record stands for 52 years.
Robert Fulton's North River Steamboat, later called the Clermont, leaves New York for Albany: 150 miles in 32 hours, with an engine by Boulton and Watt. Steam is shown to pay on the water.
At 11:30 p.m. Hurricane Camille comes ashore at Waveland, Mississippi, as a Category 5 with 175 mph winds and a 24.6-foot surge, the highest then recorded in the continental United States.
The balloon Double Eagle II lands at Miserey, near Paris, 137 hours 6 minutes out of Presque Isle, Maine. Ben Abruzzo, Maxie Anderson and Larry Newman are the first across the Atlantic by balloon.
At the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington, Asaph Hall finds Phobos, the inner moon of Mars, with the 26-inch refractor, days after finding Deimos. Phobos circles Mars in 7 hours 39 minutes.
The Soviet Union launches the dogs Belka and Strelka into orbit with forty mice and two rats. They land the next day: the first animals sent into orbit and returned safely to Earth.
At 7 p.m. The New York Times sends a cablegram from its 17th floor: 'This message sent around the world.' Relayed by 16 operators, it travels more than 28,613 miles and is back in 16.5 minutes.
Voyager 2 lifts off on a Titan IIIE, sixteen days before Voyager 1. It becomes the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune, and it enters interstellar space in 2018.
A total solar eclipse crosses the United States from the Pacific to the Atlantic, the first to do so since 1918. Totality touches 14 states, with about 2 minutes 38 seconds at Columbia, Missouri.
Watched by Queen Victoria, the New York Yacht Club's schooner America beats 15 yachts of the Royal Yacht Squadron around the Isle of Wight. The trophy becomes the America's Cup.
The city of St. Louis votes to secede from St. Louis County and become an independent city. After a recount the separation takes effect in March 1877.
The Cadillac Automobile Company is established from the remnants of the Henry Ford Company, under Henry Leland. It is named for the French explorer who founded Detroit.
Lunar Orbiter 1, the first American spacecraft to orbit the Moon, takes the first picture of the Earth from the distance of the Moon.
Hurricane Andrew hits Elliott Key, Florida, then Homestead as a Category 5 with 165 mph winds. It destroys 63,500 houses and does $27.3 billion in damage: the costliest U.S. hurricane until Katrina.
Microsoft ships Windows 95, code-named Chicago, with a Start menu, a taskbar and long file names, to the Rolling Stones' 'Start Me Up'. A million copies ship in four days.
Paris is liberated. General von Choltitz surrenders the German garrison at 3:30 p.m. at the Hotel Meurice to Leclerc's French 2nd Armored Division, which entered with the U.S. 4th Infantry Division.
Voyager 2 passes about 3,000 miles above the north pole of Neptune, twelve years after launch. No other spacecraft has visited the planet.
Linus Torvalds, 21, a student at the University of Helsinki, tells the newsgroup comp.os.minix he is writing a free operating system: 'just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu.'
Experimental station W2XBS in New York televises a major league baseball game for the first time: a doubleheader between the Cincinnati Reds and the Brooklyn Dodgers.
Erich Warsitz flies the Heinkel He 178, powered by Hans von Ohain's HeS 3 engine: the world's first aircraft to fly on the thrust of a turbojet. Germany invades Poland days later.
The likeliest date of the race between a horse-drawn car and Peter Cooper's Tom Thumb, the first American-built steam locomotive on a common-carrier railroad. The horse wins when a blower belt slips.
Kiichiro Toyoda's Toyota Motor Company is incorporated, a spinoff of his father's loom works. 'Toyota' takes eight brush strokes to write in Japanese, a lucky number.
Gottlieb Daimler patents the Reitwagen, built with Wilhelm Maybach in a garden shed at Cannstatt: the first gasoline motorcycle. Its half-horsepower engine is good for about 7 mph.
Hurricane Katrina comes ashore near Buras, Louisiana, as a Category 3 with 125 mph winds. More than 50 levee breaches flood 80 percent of New Orleans. 1,392 people die.
The second Morrill Act becomes law, granting cash to the land-grant colleges. States must show race is no bar to admission or name a separate college for African Americans. The South does the latter.
The Moscow-Washington hotline goes into operation. It is a teletype circuit, never a red telephone. Washington's first test message: THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPED OVER THE LAZY DOG'S BACK 1234567890.
Discovery lifts off at 8:41 a.m. Eastern on her maiden flight, two months after an abort four seconds before launch. The crew of six deploys three communications satellites and lands September 5.
The Detroit News station 8MK, on the air daily since August 20, broadcasts returns from that day's primary election. Now WWJ, it is believed to be the first station to broadcast news regularly.
Emma Nutt starts work at Edwin Holmes's telephone company in Boston: the world's first female telephone operator, paid $10 a month for a 54-hour week. Her sister Stella follows hours later.
St. Louis Union Station opens, designed by Theodore Link, with 32 tracks under its trainshed: at its opening the largest station in the world. Amtrak abandons it on October 31, 1978.
At 4:45 a.m. the old German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opens fire on the Polish depot at Westerplatte as Germany invades Poland. Britain and France declare war on Germany on September 3.
At 12:48 a.m. debris appears on the screens of the research ship Knorr: a boiler from the Titanic, 12,500 feet down. The French-American team is led by Jean-Louis Michel and Robert Ballard.
A great solar storm peaks. Telegraph systems across Europe and North America fail, some shocking their operators; on the Boston-Portland line messages pass for two hours with no battery at all.

The Labor Day hurricane, a Category 5 with 185 mph winds, comes ashore near Long Key, Florida. An eleven-car evacuation train is swept off the track; all aboard survive. The railroad is never rebuilt.
Aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, Foreign Minister Shigemitsu signs Japan's surrender at 9:04 a.m.; General MacArthur signs for the Allies. The ceremony lasts 23 minutes and is broadcast worldwide.
Dagen H: at 5 a.m. Sweden switches from driving on the left to the right, though in 1955 83 percent had voted to keep left. Only 157 minor accidents are reported that day.
The Viking 2 lander touches down on Mars at Utopia Planitia, about 200 km west of the crater Mie. It works on the surface until its batteries fail on April 12, 1980.
Over Labor Day weekend the first Midwest Old Threshers reunion is held at Mount Pleasant, Iowa: 15 steam engines, 8 separators and an estimated 10,000 visitors. It has run yearly since, except 2020.
The Bell System's new microwave relay now links the two coasts, in time to carry President Truman's opening address at the San Francisco peace treaty conference with Japan across the nation.
Larry Page and Sergey Brin incorporate Google in their friend Susan Wojcicki's garage in Menlo Park, California. The search engine began in 1996 as a research project nicknamed BackRub.
Voyager 1 lifts off on a Titan IIIE, sixteen days after Voyager 2. It passes Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, enters interstellar space in 2012, and is the most distant human-made object.
The Victoria, under Juan Sebastian Elcano, returns to Sanlucar, Spain: the first ship to sail around the world. Of about 270 men who left in five ships in 1519, 18 come home aboard her.
In his lab at 202 Green Street, San Francisco, Philo Farnsworth, just 21, sends the first image from his image dissector camera tube to a receiver in another room: a simple straight line.

The Blitz begins: 348 German bombers and 617 fighters attack London by day, and more bombers return that night. The city is bombed on 56 of the next 57 days and nights; the Blitz lasts until May 1941.
At 2:30 a.m. the schooner Augusta rams the steamer Lady Elgin on Lake Michigan off what is now Highland Park, Illinois. Over 300 die; a student, Edward Spencer, saves 17 people.
Near Gold Creek, Montana Territory, Henry Villard's Northern Pacific drives its ceremonial last spike before about 300 guests brought on five special trains, among them Ulysses S. Grant.
About 8 p.m. a Category 4 hurricane strikes Galveston, Texas; a surge of over 15 feet washes over the whole island. Between 6,000 and 12,000 die: the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history.
Operators of the Harvard Mark II trace an error to a moth trapped in a relay and tape it into the log book: 'First actual case of bug being found.' The log is now at the Smithsonian.
Oliver Hazard Perry's squadron defeats and captures six British ships on Lake Erie. Rowed through gunfire to the Niagara, Perry reports: 'We have met the enemy and they are ours.'
Henry Hudson, sailing for the Dutch East India Company, enters Upper New York Bay. Over ten days his ship climbs the river now named for him; a boat crew gets near present-day Albany.
At Texas Instruments, Jack Kilby shows managers a piece of germanium wired to an oscilloscope: a steady sine wave from his integrated circuit. It earns him a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics.
At Rice Stadium, Houston, before about 40,000 people, Kennedy says: 'We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.'
At West 74th Street and Central Park West in New York, Henry Bliss is struck by an electric taxicab and dies the next morning: the first recorded U.S. death in a motor vehicle collision.
The Soviet probe Luna 2 hits the Moon east of Mare Imbrium at 21:02 GMT, scattering pennants engraved USSR: the first human-made object to make contact with another celestial body.
After 25 hours of British bombardment, Fort McHenry's 30-by-42-foot flag flies over Baltimore in the morning. Francis Scott Key, watching from a truce ship, writes 'Defence of Fort M'Henry.'

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens: the world's first inter-city railway, and the first worked only by steam. On opening day the Rocket strikes William Huskisson, MP, who dies of his injuries.
The Crash at Crush: before an estimated 40,000 people, the Katy railroad runs two locomotives head-on into each other in Texas for show. Both boilers explode and two people are killed.
Battle of Britain Day: the RAF breaks up the Luftwaffe's largest attack on London. Germany loses 58 aircraft, Britain 29. Two days later Hitler postpones the invasion of Britain.
William C. Durant founds General Motors as a holding company for Buick. Olds Motor Works joins in November; Cadillac and Oakland, the forerunner of Pontiac, follow in 1909.
Steve Jobs, back at Apple since it bought his company NeXT, is formally named interim chief executive. He jokes that he will use the title 'iCEO'.
At Fort Myer, Virginia, a propeller breaks on Orville Wright's Flyer. His passenger, Lt. Thomas Selfridge, is the first person to die in an airplane crash; Wright spends seven weeks in hospital.
The space shuttle Enterprise rolls out at Palmdale, California, named after a letter campaign by Star Trek fans; most of the show's original cast attend. Built for tests, it never flies in space.
The U.S. Air Force becomes an independent service, formed from the Army Air Forces under the National Security Act of 1947. Stuart Symington takes office as its first secretary.
At 11:44 on a Carnegie Mellon bulletin board, Scott Fahlman proposes joke markers: ':-) Read it sideways.' For things that are NOT jokes, he suggests ':-('.
Ferdinand Magellan's five ships, led by the flagship Trinidad, leave Spain with about 270 men. Magellan dies in the Philippines in 1521; only Victoria, with 18 men, gets home in 1522.
Charles and Frank Duryea road-test their gasoline-powered automobile, the second built in America. In 1895 their Springfield, Mass., company becomes the first American firm to build gasoline cars.
The Long Island Express, a Category 3 hurricane racing north at 47 mph, comes ashore at Bellport, New York. It kills about 682 people; its surge puts 13 feet of water in downtown Providence.
The Four Level Interchange opens at the northern edge of downtown Los Angeles, joining U.S. 101 and State Route 110: the first stack interchange in the world. It cost $5.5 million.
Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery reaches St. Louis, home from the Pacific, 862 days after setting out from Camp Dubois on May 14, 1804.
On the night of September 23 at the Berlin Observatory, Johann Galle, helped by student Heinrich d'Arrest, finds Neptune less than one degree from where Le Verrier's mathematics put it.
Henri Giffard flies his airship 17 miles from Paris to Elancourt: the first powered and controlled flight. A 3-horsepower steam engine turns its propeller.
USS Enterprise is launched at Newport News, Virginia: the world's first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, with eight reactors. At 1,123 feet she is the longest naval vessel ever built.
TAT-1, the first transatlantic telephone cable, opens between Oban, Scotland, and Clarenville, Newfoundland. It carries 588 London-U.S. calls in its first 24 hours, and is retired in 1978.
Francis Drake's Golden Hind reaches the English Channel and sails into Plymouth with 59 crew, nearly three years out: Drake is the first Englishman to sail around the world. He is knighted in 1581.
John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon meet at the WBBM-TV studios in Chicago for the first of four debates, moderated by Howard K. Smith of CBS. Nixon's stubble shows on black-and-white screens.
The Soviet early-warning system reports one, then five U.S. missiles launched. The officer on duty, Stanislav Petrov, judges it a false alarm. The cause: sunlight on high-altitude clouds.
The Stockton and Darlington Railway opens: the world's first public railway to use steam locomotives. Locomotion No. 1 hauls 31 vehicles with 550 passengers, reaching 10 to 12 mph.
On its fourth try, SpaceX's Falcon 1 reaches orbit from Omelek Island in the Kwajalein Atoll: the first privately developed liquid-fueled rocket to do so.
A tornado rated EF4 tears through downtown St. Louis, destroying more than 200 city blocks. 79 people die and 550 are injured.
Discovery lifts off on STS-26, the Return to Flight mission, the first since the Challenger disaster, with an all-veteran crew. She deploys the TDRS-C satellite and lands October 3.
The Berlin Airlift officially ends after fifteen months: about 2.3 million tons, nearly two-thirds of it coal, flown in on 278,228 flights. The Soviets lifted the blockade on May 12.
The first Boeing 747 rolls out of the new Everett plant, the largest building by volume ever built. The first 'Jumbo Jet' flies on February 9, 1969, and enters service with Pan Am in 1970.
